cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Programme 9
cards.body: Professional nursing requires more than technical competence. Every action, conversation, record and decision reflects your accountability to patients, the profession and the wider community.

bullets.label: This programme develops the essential
bullets.text: This programme develops the essential knowledge, attitudes and behaviours required to practise safely, protect patient rights and maintain public trust — aligned with nursing regulatory bodies across different countries.

bullets.label: Explain the role and identity of the professional nurse
Apply core ethical principles to routine nursing care
Practise within scope, competence and organisational policy
Protect privacy, support consent and document care accurately
Communicate respectfully, delegate safely and reflect on practice
Patients depend on nurses not only for clinical
bullets.text: Patients depend on nurses not only for clinical care but also for honesty, advocacy, confidentiality and sound judgement.

bullets.label: An inaccurate record, an inappropriate disclosure or an unchallenged unsafe order can place patients at serious risk.
Your learning goal: consistently apply
bullets.text: Your learning goal: consistently apply professional standards, ethical principles and basic legal responsibilities within your scope of practice.

bullets.label: Professional identity is expressed through
bullets.text: Professional identity is expressed through knowledge, conduct, communication and responsibility — and it includes knowing when to seek help.

bullets.label: Delivering safe, patient-centred clinical care with compassion and skill
Speaking up for patient rights, dignity and preferences
Teaching patients, families and junior colleagues
Linking multidisciplinary teams around the patient's goals
Responsibility = duties accepted within a role.
bullets.text: Responsibility = duties accepted within a role. Accountability = being answerable for decisions and outcomes. Following an instruction does not remove the duty to question an unsafe action.

bullets.label: Shaped by law, registration, education and
bullets.text: Shaped by law, registration, education and workplace policy. Never perform unfamiliar or unauthorised activities without preparation and supervision.

bullets.label: The therapeutic relationship exists solely to
bullets.text: The therapeutic relationship exists solely to meet the patient's needs. Personal, financial or romantic relationships can create exploitation and loss of objectivity.

cards.title: CLINICAL EXAMPLE · SECTION 1
cards.body: A newly qualified nurse is asked to manage an unfamiliar central-line procedure alone. Rather than pretending competence, the nurse explains the limitation, reviews the procedure and requests supervised practice.

bullets.label: Prevents a potential harm from inexperience
Honest self-assessment is a mark of professionalism
Requests guided practice rather than guessing
Ethical principles guide consent,
bullets.text: Ethical principles guide consent, truth-telling, advocacy, privacy and treatment decisions — they are everyday tools, not abstract theory.

bullets.label: The patient's right to make informed decisions — including choices professionals may not prefer
Actively promoting good outcomes and the patient's wellbeing
Avoiding or minimising harm; balancing benefit against burden and risk
Fairness, equal respect and appropriate distribution of care and resources
Keeping professional commitments and communicating honestly — false reassurance weakens trust
When ethical principles conflict, seek guidance from senior colleagues, ethics committees or professional guidelines.
Legal and professional duties protect patients
bullets.text: Legal and professional duties protect patients from unwanted treatment, privacy breaches and unsafe continuity of care. These three pillars are core nursing responsibilities.

bullets.label: Requires capacity, adequate information and voluntariness
Share information only for legitimate care purposes
Timely, accurate, factual and attributable records
A person with capacity may refuse treatment.
bullets.text: A person with capacity may refuse treatment. Assess understanding, explore concerns, notify the clinician and document without coercion.

bullets.label: Records must show assessment, action, response
bullets.text: Records must show assessment, action, response and escalation. Never alter records deceptively or complete them in advance.

bullets.label: Conversations in public spaces, casual
bullets.text: Conversations in public spaces, casual messaging and social-media posts can all breach patient confidentiality — even without naming a patient.

bullets.text: A relative phones requesting test results. The nurse cannot confirm authority and explains that information cannot be disclosed, then follows the organisation's process for authorised communication.

bullets.label: Professional nursing depends on clear
bullets.text: Professional nursing depends on clear communication, safe teamwork and the willingness to reflect. Delegation improves care — but accountability always remains with the registered nurse.

bullets.label: Clear, respectful and patient-safety focused. Neither passive silence nor aggressive blame.
Right task, right person, right direction, right supervision. Clinical judgement stays with the registered nurse.
Use facts, patient needs and approved pathways. Hierarchy should never prevent speaking up.
Examines what happened, why and how to improve — supporting resilience and professional growth.
By completing GNPS Programme 9 — Level 1, you
bullets.text: By completing GNPS Programme 9 — Level 1, you have built the foundational capabilities to practise accountably, apply ethical principles, protect patient rights and communicate professionally. You are now prepared for Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse, where these principles are applied within diverse legal, cultural and regulatory systems.

bullets.label: Ethics, legal accountability and professional practice are high-yield NCLEX domains

decks.title: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 9 - Level 1 - Section 1 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Programme Overview
cards.body: Section 1: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability

bullets.label: Professional identity is expressed through
bullets.text: Professional identity is expressed through knowledge, conduct, communication and responsibility. This section explores what it means to be a professionally accountable nurse in everyday clinical practice.

bullets.label: Your professional identity as a nurse

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Describe the roles of the professional nurse

cards.title: The Many Roles of a Professional Nurse
cards.body: Nurses operate across multiple interconnected roles — each requiring respectful communication, sound clinical judgement and a focus on patient goals.

bullets.label: Delivers safe, compassionate, evidence-based care to patients and their families.
Speaks up for patient rights, dignity and informed decision-making at every stage.
Teaches patients, families and peers — empowering them with health knowledge.
Organises multidisciplinary care to ensure seamless, patient-centred outcomes.
Partners with the wider healthcare team to achieve shared goals for patient welfare.
Responsibility refers to the duties accepted within your nursing role — the tasks and care you agree to carry out.
Accountability means being answerable for your
bullets.text: Accountability means being answerable for your decisions and the outcomes they produce — even when you were following an instruction.

bullets.label: Following an instruction does not remove your duty to question an unsafe action.
Owning the outcomes of your decisions
Answering to patients, employers and regulators
Both concepts work together. You cannot separate what you do from your duty to own the outcome of those actions.

cards.title: Scope of Practice and Competence
cards.body: Your scope of practice is not fixed — it is shaped by multiple intersecting factors that define the boundaries of safe, authorised nursing activity.

cards.title: What Shapes Your Scope?
cards.body: Scope is a dynamic boundary — it can expand with further training and supervision, or narrow in practice settings where competence has not been demonstrated.

bullets.label: Nurses must never perform unfamiliar or
bullets.text: Nurses must never perform unfamiliar or unauthorised activities without appropriate preparation, supervision and employer sanction.

bullets.label: The therapeutic relationship exists solely to
bullets.text: The therapeutic relationship exists solely to meet the patient's needs. It is built on trust, professionalism and the deliberate management of power dynamics.

bullets.label: Boundary violations — whether personal, financial, romantic or dual-role relationships — can cause:
Loss of professional standing and registration
Forming close friendships with patients blurs
bullets.text: Forming close friendships with patients blurs the line between therapeutic care and personal connection, undermining clinical objectivity.

bullets.label: Accepting gifts, loans or financial
bullets.text: Accepting gifts, loans or financial arrangements from patients or families creates conflicts of interest and ethical obligations.

bullets.label: Any romantic interest or pre-existing personal
bullets.text: Any romantic interest or pre-existing personal relationship with a patient compromises the integrity of professional care delivery.

bullets.label: Sharing patient information or engaging with
bullets.text: Sharing patient information or engaging with patients online — even with good intent — can constitute a serious professional boundary violation.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: A newly qualified nurse is asked to manage an unfamiliar central-line procedure — alone. Rather than pretending competence, the nurse explains the limitation, reviews the procedure and requests supervised practice.

bullets.label: This decision protects the patient and demonstrates genuine accountability in action.

cards.title: Unpacking the Clinical Example
cards.body: What Accountability Looks Like in Practice

bullets.label: Accountable practice is not about knowing
bullets.text: Accountable practice is not about knowing everything — it is about being honest when you do not, and taking the right steps to protect your patient and your professional integrity.

bullets.label: Professionalism is shown through consistent conduct, not exceptional moments alone.
Practise only within your competence, registration and workplace-sanctioned boundaries.
Challenge unsafe instructions calmly and professionally — patient safety is always the priority.
Maintain clear therapeutic boundaries in every patient and professional interaction.
Caregiver, advocate, educator, coordinator and collaborator — each demands professional conduct.
You are answerable for your decisions and outcomes — regardless of who gave the instruction.
Law, registration, competence and workplace policy all define your safe boundaries of practice.
Professional boundaries preserve patient trust, dignity and your registration as a nurse.

decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 9 - Level 1 - Section 2 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

bullets.label: Section 2: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights

cards.title: What Are Ethical Principles?
cards.body: Ethical principles help nurses reason through choices that affect dignity, safety and fairness. They are not abstract ideas — they guide everyday practice.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Articulate the major ethical principles underpinning nursing practice.
Honour patient autonomy and support informed decision-making.
Uphold patient dignity and ensure equitable care delivery.
Identify when ethical principles come into tension and seek appropriate support.
Autonomy recognises every person's right to
bullets.text: Autonomy recognises every person's right to make informed decisions about their own care — including decisions that healthcare professionals may not prefer.

bullets.label: Ensuring patients have sufficient, clear information
Accepting refusal as a valid, protected choice
Advocating for the patient's expressed wishes
Autonomy applies to competent adults. Capacity must always be assessed before proceeding.
Promote good. Act in the patient's best interest. Provide evidence-based care that genuinely benefits the individual.
Avoid harm. Minimise risk, side effects and unnecessary burden. "First, do no harm" remains a guiding standard.
Nurses routinely weigh potential benefit
bullets.text: Nurses routinely weigh potential benefit against burden and risk — for example, when administering a treatment with significant side effects.

bullets.label: Fair, equal treatment and appropriate distribution of care and resources — regardless of background or status.
Keeping professional commitments. Patients must be able to trust that nurses follow through on their word.
Honesty in all communications. False reassurance or withholding information weakens therapeutic trust.

cards.title: How the Principles Interconnect
cards.body: No single principle operates in isolation. Skilled nurses navigate all five simultaneously, weighing priorities when tensions arise.

cards.title: Clinical Example in Practice
cards.body: A competent patient refuses a blood transfusion based on deeply held personal beliefs.

bullets.label: Clearly relay decision to the team.
Throughout each step, respect for autonomy
bullets.text: Throughout each step, respect for autonomy remains central. The nurse acts as the patient's advocate — not the gatekeeper of their choices.

bullets.label: Ethical principles provide a reliable framework for complex clinical decisions.
Respect informed decisions — including a patient's right to refuse treatment.
Veracity and fidelity are non-negotiable foundations of the nurse–patient relationship.
When principles conflict, escalate appropriately — never navigate ethical dilemmas alone.

decks.title: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 9 - Level 1 - Section 3 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Mastering Essential Clinical Skills
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 10 · Level 1

bullets.label: Legal and professional responsibilities
bullets.text: Legal and professional responsibilities safeguard patients from unwanted treatment, privacy breaches, and unsafe continuity of care. Informed consent, confidentiality, and accurate documentation are not optional — they are core nursing obligations that protect both patients and practitioners.

bullets.label: Protecting private information at all times
Ensuring safe, accurate continuity of care

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify the essential elements that make consent valid and legally sound
Apply confidentiality principles across all care settings and communication channels
Record assessments, actions and responses objectively and promptly
Identify common pitfalls that expose nurses and patients to harm
Valid consent rests on three essential pillars. All three must be present for consent to be legally and ethically sound.
Nurses may witness consent or support patient
bullets.text: Nurses may witness consent or support patient understanding — but must not provide clinical explanations outside their role.

bullets.label: The patient can understand, retain, and weigh information to make a decision
Adequate, relevant information is provided in a way the patient can understand
The decision is made freely, without pressure or coercion
A patient with decision-making capacity has the
bullets.text: A patient with decision-making capacity has the legal right to refuse any treatment, even if clinicians believe it is in their best interest. The nurse's role is to support, not override, this right.

bullets.label: Confirm the patient comprehends the consequences of refusal
Listen actively and address any fears or misconceptions
Escalate immediately to the appropriate medical practitioner
Record the discussion factually, without personal opinion or coercion
Patient information must be accessed and shared
bullets.text: Patient information must be accessed and shared only for legitimate care purposes. Any disclosure beyond this boundary constitutes a breach — with professional and legal consequences.

bullets.label: Discussing patient details in corridors, lifts, or public areas
Sending clinical information via casual messaging apps
Posting patient-related content on social media — even without names
Sharing records with family members without patient authority
The record is the legal and clinical account of care delivered. If it is not documented, it did not happen.
Documented promptly — as close to the event as possible
Reflects exactly what was observed, said and done
States objective findings — not assumptions or personal opinions
Clearly identifies who documented what and when
Records must never be altered deceptively or
bullets.text: Records must never be altered deceptively or completed in advance. Falsification of records is a serious professional and criminal offence.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: A Phone Call About Test Results

bullets.label: Scenario: A relative telephones the ward requesting the patient's test results.
The Challenge: The nurse cannot confirm the caller's identity or their authority to receive confidential information.
Politely explain that information cannot be
bullets.text: Politely explain that information cannot be disclosed without verified authority — regardless of the relationship claimed

bullets.label: Direct the caller to the organisation's authorised communication process
Record the call, the request made and the action taken
Must be informed, voluntary and given by a person with capacity
Share information only with verified, appropriate authority
Record facts, not opinions — promptly and without alteration
Never discuss, post about, or photograph patient care online
Global Nursing Professional Series · GNPS Program 10

decks.title: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 9 - Level 1 - Section 4 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Mastering Essential Clinical Skills
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 10 · Level 1

bullets.label: Section 4: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
Professional nursing depends on clear
bullets.text: Professional nursing depends on clear communication, safe teamwork, and a genuine willingness to reflect. Delegation can significantly improve patient care — but the nurse always remains responsible for assessing whether the task, person, and circumstances are appropriate.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Express clinical concerns clearly and respectfully in all care settings.
Use the five rights of delegation to assign tasks safely and appropriately.
Navigate conflict professionally using facts, evidence, and escalation pathways.
Use structured reflection to support continuous professional development.
Assertive communication is clear, respectful,
bullets.text: Assertive communication is clear, respectful, and focused on patient safety. It occupies the professional middle ground between passive silence and aggressive blame.

bullets.label: Stays silent; avoids confrontation even when patient safety is at risk.
States concerns calmly, uses facts, and advocates for the patient.
Blames or threatens; damages team trust and care quality.
Safe delegation is guided by five rights.
bullets.text: Safe delegation is guided by five rights. Assessment, clinical judgement, teaching, and evaluation always remain with the registered nurse.

bullets.label: Is this task appropriate to delegate within policy and scope?
Is the patient stable and the setting safe for delegation?
Is the team member trained and competent for this task?
Have clear, specific instructions been given?
Is appropriate follow-up and oversight in place?
Delegation transfers a task — not accountability. The registered nurse retains professional responsibility at all times.
Disagreement is a normal part of clinical
bullets.text: Disagreement is a normal part of clinical teamwork. Nurses must address conflict using facts, patient needs, and approved escalation pathways — never allowing hierarchy to prevent speaking up when safety is at risk.

bullets.label: Focus on the clinical concern, not the individual.
Follow your organisation's escalation protocol without hesitation.
Reflection examines what happened, why it
bullets.text: Reflection examines what happened, why it happened, and what could improve. It is the foundation of professional resilience and ongoing development.

bullets.label: Structured reflection — such as Gibbs'
bullets.text: Structured reflection — such as Gibbs' Reflective Cycle — transforms everyday clinical experiences into lasting professional learning and supports NCLEX-style critical thinking.

bullets.label: Registered nurse identifies a stable patient
bullets.text: Registered nurse identifies a stable patient suitable for routine observations and selects an appropriately trained assistant.

bullets.label: Nurse provides precise instructions, defines normal parameters, and confirms the assistant understands the task.
Assistant reports a change in observations. Nurse reassesses the patient immediately and adjusts the care plan.
Nurse documents the episode and reflects on decision-making to strengthen future delegation practice.

cards.title: NCLEX Focus
cards.body: Key Points for Competitive Exam Success

bullets.label: The RN delegates the task but retains full professional accountability.
Vague delegation is unsafe delegation. Always give specific parameters and follow up.
Address disagreement with clinical facts and patient-centred reasoning.
Use structured reflection after challenging situations to drive continuous improvement.

cards.title: Section 4 Complete
cards.body: You have covered the essential principles of professional communication, delegation, conflict management, and reflective practice — all critical competencies for safe nursing and NCLEX success.

bullets.label: Assertively and respectfully in every clinical interaction.
Using the five rights — and always follow up.
To grow professionally and strengthen future decision-making.
